I am 65 years old and have farmed in Quzhou County my whole life. I never went to school, but I know this land and this climate better than any book. Every year, I grow winter wheat and summer maize on my 5 mu. It is the only system that makes sense here on the North China Plain — wheat goes in after National Day in October, comes out in early June, and maize goes in the same day and comes out in October before the cold. I use rotary tillage before wheat sowing because the tractor man from the village charges 50 yuan per mu and it prepares a good seedbed. For wheat, I buy improved seed from the supply shop, about 30 jin per mu. I spread compound fertilizer before sowing and topdress with urea in spring when the wheat turns green. I irrigate four times: winter irrigation to keep the wheat alive through the cold, then twice in spring, and once before grain filling. I spray when I see aphids or weeds. For maize, I sow hybrid seed directly into the wheat stubble right after harvest — no need to till, the stubble keeps moisture and saves me labor. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing. Maize needs less fuss: two irrigations, one at jointing and one at tasseling, and three pesticide sprays for armyworm and weeds. I expect about 1000 kg per mu for wheat and 1100 kg per mu for maize. I eat some, give some to my children who work in the city, and sell the rest to the grain buyer who drives to the village. I do not grow cotton anymore — my hands are not steady enough for the pruning, and the pesticide sprays are too many for my old back. Wheat and maize are stable, the buyers come every year, and I know exactly how to manage them.
